items.title: [esa.int] Hubble and Webb expose hidden structures in Carina star-forming cloud
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

NASA’s Hubble and James Webb space telescopes have captured complementary views of the Cat’s Head Nebula, a star-forming pillar in the Carina Nebula about 7,500 light-years from Earth. Hubble’s visible-light image shows a dark dust column edged by glowing gas, while Webb’s infrared observations reveal details within the dust, including stars and fine strands. The images, released Oct. 29, help astronomers examine how young stars form in gas and dust exposed to radiation from massive nearby stars. Ultraviolet radiation and stellar winds likely shaped the pillar’s outline by eroding its surroundings, while denser material resisted erosion. Webb also imaged the lower-metallicity N159 star-forming region in the Large Magellanic Cloud, while Chandra and Webb observations show young stars forming in a separate Carina cloud.

items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

For nearly 90 years, scientists believed magnetism fell into just two categories, but researchers have now confirmed a remarkable third type called altermagnetism. Using specialized X-rays, they uncovered a unique magnetic signature that proves these materials behave differently from conventional magnets. Altermagnets combine stability with the ability to efficiently carry information, potentially overcoming major limitations in today's electronics. The discovery could lead to faster computers, more efficient data centers, and breakthroughs in quantum technology.

items.title: [sci.news] CERN experiment reports first evidence of ultra-rare beauty meson decay
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

The LHCb collaboration at CERN reported the first evidence of a neutral beauty meson (B⁰) decaying into two muons, a process predicted to occur about once in every 10 billion such particles. Combining the new result with earlier LHCb data gave the signal a statistical significance of 3.2 standard deviations—enough to count as evidence, but below the five-standard-deviation threshold for a discovery. The measured rate is consistent with the Standard Model, the leading theory of particle physics. Rare decays can be sensitive to effects from particles that are not produced directly in collisions. Researchers plan to continue collecting data into the early 2030s to refine the measurement; a further detector upgrade is also planned.

items.title: [sciencefeatured.com] Higher BMI over time linked to faster cognitive decline in older adults
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

A 24-year study of several thousand middle-aged and older Americans found that higher average body mass index (BMI) over time was associated with faster declines in memory and thinking. A team led by University of Georgia researcher Suhang Song reported the findings in the Journal of Neurology. The association was strongest when cognitive abilities were assessed about eight years after weight measurements and was more pronounced among participants who were older when the study began. The observational study cannot establish that higher weight causes cognitive decline or that weight loss would prevent it. The researchers noted that participants reported their own height and weight and that the analysis could not account for physical activity. The team called for further research into possible biological mechanisms and future interventions.

items.title: [phys.org] UN warns warming will breach 1.5C as COP31 opens Monday
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

The United Nations says global warming will exceed the 1.5-degree Celsius threshold as nearly 200 countries prepare to begin the COP31 climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, on Nov. 9. Climate scientists say the rate of warming has effectively doubled over the past decade. October 2026 was the hottest October on record, and 2026 is virtually certain to become the second year to exceed 1.5C, after 2024. U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres said the world must now limit how far temperatures rise beyond that level and blamed political leaders for failing to act. The Nov. 9-20 talks are expected to focus on fulfilling earlier promises to move away from fossil fuels and on funding for poorer countries facing climate impacts. Turkey is promoting a goal to increase electricity’s share of global energy demand from about 20% to 35% by 2035. Developed countries have resisted further funding commitments, and the Trump administration is not taking part in negotiations.

items.title: [science.org] JWST image-processing method boosts exoplanet sensitivity up to 15-fold
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Astronomers have developed a physics-based method to remove residual starlight from James Webb Space Telescope images, improving sensitivity to faint planets by two to 15 times and revealing the known giant exoplanet 51 Eridani b at a wavelength where earlier processing failed. The method, called Physics-based Learning for Imaging Planets, or FLIP, models the telescope’s optics and adjusts for small changes that make conventional reference-star images imperfect matches. The method works with existing observations without changes to telescope hardware. The team is now reprocessing the hundreds of coronagraphic images JWST has collected to look for additional planets. Researchers say the approach could ease strict stability requirements for future observatories, but further work is needed to reduce computing costs and test it on larger data sets.

items.title: [abcnews.com] Swift telescope shutdown ends rapid alerts for cosmic explosions
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

NASA shut down its Swift Observatory in late October after it could no longer hold steady enough for observations, ending a 22-year mission to detect gamma-ray bursts, supernovas and other high-energy events. Swift’s rapid observations helped direct other space telescopes toward eruptions for more detailed study, and astronomers are working out how to replace that alert function. The observatory resumed observations after the rescue effort ended and captured additional gamma-ray bursts and other ultrahigh-energy events before NASA turned off its systems. Over its mission, Swift recorded more than 2,000 gamma-ray bursts and 1,400 exploding stars.

items.title: [phys.org] Extra schooling under UK reform linked to fewer dementia diagnoses
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

A study of more than 100,000 UK Biobank participants found that a 1972 British law requiring teenagers to stay in school until 16 was associated with fewer diagnoses of Alzheimer’s disease and related dementias nearly 50 years later. Using the reform’s September 1, 1957, birth-date cutoff, researchers compared people subject to different school-leaving rules and reported a 0.88% reduction in dementia incidence among those affected. Researchers also found the reduction among participants with high genetic susceptibility. They cautioned that dementia was uncommon in this cohort, whose diagnoses were tracked only through age 65, making the estimate imprecise. Continued follow-up will help determine whether the difference persists as participants age.

items.title: [sciencealert.com] Octopus study maps two tactics for squeezing through tight openings
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Researchers have documented how common octopuses change their movements to pass through small openings, adding a step when a gap is narrower than the distance between their eyes. For the study, published in the Journal of Experimental Biology, researchers filmed octopuses probing openings with an arm, passing other arms through, then using them to pull the rest of the body through. In tighter gaps, the animals passed their remaining arms through before squeezing the mantle and head through separately. The experiments included three subadult common octopuses. A report on the study also described tests involving four Mayan octopuses, which did not attempt to pass through the narrower openings. The researchers say the movement patterns could inform the design of soft robots for search and rescue, where current slender designs leave limited room for equipment. An octopus-like robot would need flexible arms that can both squeeze through gaps and pull the rest of the machine forward.

items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

A team led by University of Washington astronomer Mario Juric has identified a possible dwarf planet in early data from Chile’s Vera C. Rubin Observatory and estimates it is 1,000 to 2,000 miles across. The object, provisionally designated 2026 ED-138, lies about 46 astronomical units from Earth; the team also found it in older observations, including photographic plates dating to the 1930s. The estimated size would make it far larger than the asteroids the survey team usually detects, but astronomers have not established that it is round, a requirement for dwarf-planet status. Because it is too distant for researchers to image its shape directly, they plan to study how it dims stars as it passes in front of them; one such event may occur within days, Juric said. He expects confirmation to take about two years.

items.title: [sciencedaily.com] Researchers identify heme in 115-million-year-old Brazilian dinosaur fossil
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

An international research team says it has found mineralized structures resembling red blood cells and heme, a molecule associated with hemoglobin, in a 115-million-year-old Aratasaurus museunacionali fossil from northeastern Brazil. The team describes the findings, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, as the first chemical confirmation of heme-derived molecules inside structures interpreted as dinosaur blood cells. The team says the structures lay inside the bone’s vascular canals and that the surrounding sediment lacked the same heme signature. It proposes that the mineral hausmannite helped preserve the structures and associated molecules; rapid burial in a low-oxygen setting may also have slowed decay. Paleontologist Mary Schweitzer, who was not involved in the study, disputes whether the evidence definitively identifies heme within the cell-like structures, noting that the chemical analysis covered the whole bone. The researchers say fossilization may have distorted the structures’ shape and that further work is needed to interpret it.

items.title: [scitechdaily.com] Study suggests Neptune formed from materials that originated closer to the young Sun
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Neptune may have formed from building blocks that originated closer to the young Sun before moving outward, according to research published in Astronomy & Astrophysics. Neptune’s deep atmosphere appears considerably richer in oxygen than Uranus’s, despite the planets’ similar size and mass, suggesting different chemical histories. Researchers used carbon monoxide measurements and atmospheric models to infer the planets’ hidden chemistry; they cannot directly sample the deep atmospheres. The proposed formation pathway therefore depends on models. Future spacecraft observations or atmospheric probes could help test it. NASA’s planned Uranus Orbiter and Probe is expected to launch sometime in the next decade.

Record October tides flooded roads, homes and businesses along California’s coast this week, prompting warnings that storms during El Niño could worsen flooding. In Marin County, drivers were rescued from flooded cars and kayakers crossed streets; in Newport Beach, flooding blocked access to a local boat company’s dock. Researchers attribute the high water to rising seas, unusually warm ocean water, El Niño-linked Kelvin waves and the lunar tide cycle. Higher tides are predicted for December, when king tides and winter storms could bring further coastal flooding, though the effects will depend on their timing. The San Francisco Bay Conservation and Development Commission is using risk maps to help local officials plan, while Newport Beach is distributing sandbags.

items.title: [news.un.org] UN says record greenhouse gases lock in centuries-long warming
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

The World Meteorological Organization (WMO), the United Nations’ weather agency, reported that atmospheric concentrations of carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide all reached record levels in 2025. Carbon dioxide averaged 426.8 parts per million, methane 1,948 parts per billion and nitrous oxide 339.1 parts per billion—153%, 267% and 126% of pre-industrial levels, respectively. The annual bulletin measures gases accumulated in the atmosphere, not emissions released during the year. About half of annual carbon dioxide emissions remain in the atmosphere. The WMO says the gases’ heat-trapping effect will drive warming for decades or centuries; the past 11 years were the warmest on record. Carbon dioxide rose 2.8 parts per million from 2024 to 2025, below the previous year’s 3.6-ppm increase but still above the decade average of 2.6 ppm. The WMO linked the slower increase partly to recovering land carbon sinks and fewer fire emissions after the 2023-24 El Niño. It warned that concentrations could rise further in 2026 as fossil-fuel use continues and another powerful El Niño affects land sinks. The bulletin will inform negotiators at the Nov. 9-20 COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye.

items.title: [abc.net.au] Lancet researchers urge health emergency declaration as climate losses mount
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Heat-related disruption cost the world an estimated $1.07 trillion in lost worker productivity in 2025, while extreme drought affected about 52% of global land for at least a month, according to the 2026 Lancet Countdown report. The report’s 146 researchers from 30 countries urged governments to treat climate change as a global health emergency and coordinate a sustained response. Extreme rainfall affected 17.2% of global land each year from 2016 to 2025, up from 14.8% in the preceding decade, and the researchers linked shifting groundwater conditions to risks for food security and sanitation. Southeast Asia and Africa suffered the largest productivity-related economic losses, equivalent to 3.9% and 3.2% of gross domestic product, respectively. Clean-energy investment reached $2.1 trillion in 2025, nearly twice fossil-fuel investment, but fossil fuels still supplied more than 80% of global energy. The report calls for governments to consider health in climate decisions and direct climate and health funding to vulnerable countries. Researchers are expected to press the issue at the COP31 climate conference in Antalya, Türkiye, scheduled for Nov. 9-20.

items.title: [cw39.com] Researchers favor permanent standard time as US debates clock changes
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Most U.S. clocks turn back one hour Nov. 1, as new research reviews renew debate over whether year-round standard time or daylight saving time better supports health. A Canadian policy analysis and a review focused on people with mental illness argue that permanent standard time better protects sleep, mood and biological rhythms. A broader review of population studies, however, finds a mix of harms and benefits from seasonal clock changes and summer daylight saving time. Permanent daylight saving time would delay winter sunrise, while permanent standard time would bring earlier summer sunrises and winter sunsets. The U.S. House passed a bill to make daylight saving time permanent in July 2026, but the Senate has not taken it up. The next seasonal clock change is scheduled for March 14, 2027.

A year after the remnants of Typhoon Halong destroyed homes and infrastructure in western Alaska, residents of Kipnuk and Kwigillingok remain displaced as repairs continue, with many unsure when they can return. items.title: [LoRaMeshDevices] DIY Meshtastic Solar Node: Muziworks Uno Full Build Guide
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

A bare Meshtastic board, a battery and a solar panel are a good start. To turn them into something I can leave outside, I want a proper enclosure, a secure mounting arrangement, an external antenna and sealed cable entries. For this build, I’m using the Elecrow Muziworks Muzi Base Uno. I already had the small solar panel wired up and the basic configuration working. Now I’m putting everything into a weatherproof case, updating the firmware and getting the node ready for an outdoor test. The big question is the solar panel. It is very small, and I’m not yet convinced it will keep the battery charged. This is a working build ready for testing, not a proven, indefinitely self-sufficient solar installation. Key Takeaways Update and verify the firmware before enclosing the board, while USB access is easy. Plan the internal layout around USB clearance, battery-connector access and safe assembly. Seal every new enclosure opening, including the solar-wire entry behind the panel. Successful mesh communication does not prove the small solar panel can sustain the node. Table of Contents Parts and Layout Update the Meshtastic Firmware First Make a Small 3D-Printed Board Mount Prepare the Enclosure and External Connections Mount the Board and Battery Route, Solder and Attach the Solar Panel Seal the Cable Entry and Check the Finished Layout Configure the Node for a Fixed Installation Run a Traceroute Before Mounting Outside Put It Outside and Test the Solar Side Parts and Layout The Uno does not have the Wi-Fi capability of the Duo, which suits what I want from this solar node. It also came with a small three-wire battery, including a sensing wire rather than just the usual positive and negative connections. Here is what I used: Muzi Base Uno and its supplied battery. A weatherproof enclosure with rear mounting hardware and an internal mounting plate. A small solar panel, already connected during the earlier setup. An SMA male to N female bulkhead adapter for the external antenna connection. A larger 915 MHz external antenna. A gasketed enclosure breather plug. A custom 3D-printed board mount, small screws, 3M double-sided mounting tape and silicone sealant. The linked parts are affiliate links, which means I may earn from qualifying purchases. Before fixing anything down, check the whole layout. The board needs room for its antenna connection, battery plug and solar wiring. Just as importantly, leave enough clearance to connect a USB cable for future firmware updates. A neat installation is not much use if you have to dismantle it every time you need access. Update the Meshtastic Firmware First I did the firmware update before putting the board in the enclosure. It is much easier to work with the USB connection while everything is still on the bench. Connect the antenna before powering the board. I kept that same order later when connecting the battery. Connect the Uno to the computer with a USB cable. Open the Meshtastic web flasher at flasher.meshtastic.org. Select Muziworks, then the Muzi Base Uno/Duo device entry. Select the firmware version and start the flashing process. Follow the prompt to put the nRF-based board into DFU mode. When the board appears as a removable drive, download the matching UF2 firmware file. Copy the UF2 file onto that drive and wait for the transfer to finish. I chose Meshtastic 2.8.2 alpha for this build. That was a deliberate choice to try the newer firmware, not a recommendation to treat an alpha release as stable. The flasher offered different release channels, so check what you are selecting rather than simply assuming the newest option is the best one. Before copying the new firmware over, I also saved a copy of the existing UF2 file from the device drive to my computer. That gave me a local copy of the old firmware. I would not treat that as a separate backup of all the device settings. Once the copy completed, the drive ejected and disappeared as the board restarted. I reconnected in the Meshtastic app and checked the device details. The firmware version now showed 2.8.2, which confirmed the update had worked. Take an Initial Noise Reading The newer firmware exposed an antenna noise reading that I wanted to try. With the little stock antenna attached, the app reported approximately -97 dBm and displayed the result in green. That gave me a useful starting point before changing the enclosure and antenna. It is a noise-floor reading, though, not a range test or a measurement of antenna gain. For noise, a more negative value means a lower noise level: -97 dBm is quieter than -83 dBm. Make a Small 3D-Printed Board Mount I like mounting the board on a small raised plate rather than fixing it directly against the bottom of the enclosure. It keeps the installation tidier and leaves some space underneath the components. For this one, I drew a basic sketch with the dimensions I needed and used AI to help turn it into a printable mount. The result was an STL file that I opened in the slicer, checked and printed in PETG. The mounting-hole spacing came out correctly, and the board fitted the printed part. I used three small screws to secure it. The printed mount is optional. What matters is keeping the board secure, clear of the enclosure floor and accessible enough to maintain. There was one detail I would improve in another version: make the battery connector easier to reach after the board is mounted. That became awkward during assembly. Prepare the Enclosure and External Connections I have used this style of enclosure on other outdoor nodes without problems, so it is a familiar starting point. The supplied brackets attach to the back for mounting against a wall or another support. The case also came with cable-entry fittings, but I did not need those for this layout. Instead, I made openings for: The antenna bulkhead at the top. The breather plug on the side. The solar-panel wires behind the panel. I drilled the antenna and breather openings first. The solar-wire hole came later in my assembly, although planning all the openings before installing the electronics would make the job simpler. Fit the Breather Plug The breather plug is there to help manage moisture inside the enclosure. I am not using it as a cooling vent. It passes through the side wall and tightens against a rubber gasket. I seated the gasket against the case and tightened the fitting so it sat securely. Fit the Antenna Bulkhead The antenna connection uses an SMA male to N female bulkhead arrangement. Check the actual connector contacts as well as the threads: in this build, the SMA pin mates with the socket on the board’s antenna connection. The bulkhead passes through the top of the enclosure and has its own rubber gasket. Tightening the retaining hardware compresses that gasket against the case. The antenna and breather fittings are in place before the electronics go into the case. I then fitted the larger 915 MHz antenna to the outside. The N connector gives me a substantial external connection rather than leaving the small board-level connection exposed. Mount the Board and Battery With the external fittings installed, I checked the internal layout again. I positioned the printed mount low enough in the case to preserve USB access, with the battery beside it and room to route the antenna and solar wiring. I used two strips of 3M double-sided tape beneath the printed mount. I have had good results with this tape on other outdoor builds, so I used it again for the mount, battery and panel. Getting the backing off the tape is usually the part that tests my patience. This time, it was not too bad. The more important difficulty was the battery connector. I initially had the board attached to the mount, then removed it again because I was bending the cable and making the assembly awkward to handle. With the mount fixed down, I connected the antenna, plugged in the battery and taped the battery into the middle of the case. Everything fitted, but reinstalling the board screws while it was powered made me uncomfortable. A dropped screw could short the board. That is the part of this assembly I would change: finish the screw work with power disconnected. A better connector-access cutout in the mount, or a suitable power switch, would make the build much easier to work on. There is no prize for trying to balance tiny screws over a live board. Route, Solder and Attach the Solar Panel The panel sits on the outside of the lid. To get its wires through the enclosure, I disconnected the panel leads, drilled a small hole behind its intended position and passed the wires through. I then soldered the leads back onto the panel, keeping positive and negative on their correct connections. Check the panel position against the lid. Route the wires through the opening behind the panel. Reconnect the positive and negative leads. Check that the wires and solder joints do not prevent the panel from sitting properly. Attach the panel with mounting tape. Seal the wire opening with silicone. I ran into a small problem here: the solder connection on the back of the panel stood proud enough to stop it sitting flat against the lid. The first two strips of tape did not provide enough clearance. I adjusted the mounting with additional tape so the panel could sit properly without rocking on the solder joint. It is worth checking that clearance before pressing the adhesive down firmly. The panel’s rating was not clearly established during this build, so I am not going to give it a definite wattage or current specification. It is simply a very small panel, and its ability to keep this node running still needs an outdoor test. Seal the Cable Entry and Check the Finished Layout The antenna bulkhead and breather plug have gaskets, but the solar-wire hole needs separate sealing. I used silicone around that opening to keep water from entering along the wires. The hole is behind the solar panel, which gives it some shelter, but that is not a substitute for sealing it. Before closing the lid, I checked the main items: The board and battery were secured. The antenna connection was attached. The solar leads were connected and routed inside the case. The USB port remained accessible. The external fittings were tightened and the wire entry was sealed. At this point, the node was assembled in an enclosure intended for outdoor use. That is different from having a verified waterproof rating for the modified build. The drilled openings and seals still need to hold up in practice. Configure the Node for a Fixed Installation Back in the Meshtastic app, I requested another noise reading with the external antenna connected. It returned approximately -97 dBm, much like the stock antenna reading on the bench. That was encouraging, but it did not demonstrate a range improvement. The node was still indoors, and a noise reading alone cannot tell me how well a rooftop installation will perform. I initially left the device in Client mode. For this fixed-node experiment, I then changed the role to Client Base, selected the option to rebroadcast everything and saved the settings. The node restarted and reappeared in the app. Those are the settings I chose for this installation, rather than a claim that every solar-powered Meshtastic node should use exactly the same configuration. Run a Traceroute Before Mounting Outside For a basic connectivity check, I tried a traceroute to a nearby node down the street. The request reached it directly, while the reply came back through a different path. That confirmed the assembled node could communicate on the mesh. I then stood the enclosure upright so the antenna was vertical instead of lying along the desk and repeated the test. The displayed link reading improved from roughly -11 dB to -9 dB. It was a useful reminder to test the antenna in its intended orientation, but it was still only a short bench check, not a measured outdoor range test. Put It Outside and Test the Solar Side For the first outdoor trial, I mounted the enclosure on the side of my garden shed. This is not its final position. I wanted an accessible place to see whether the whole assembly worked before moving it to a roof. The shed mount is a temporary test position before a possible roof installation. By then, the solar-panel mounting had been sorted out, the case was closed and the node was running. Firmware flashing, the external antenna connection and the initial mesh checks had all worked. The unresolved part is the energy budget. I need to leave it outside over the next few days and find out whether that little panel can keep up with the node’s consumption. For now, I have a tidy, enclosed Meshtastic solar-node build ready for that test. If the panel proves too small, that will be the next thing to change. Getting the hardware assembled is one milestone; proving that it can stay running outside is the next one.

items.title: [digitechbytes.com] METR says Anthropic may have crossed AI acceleration warning threshold in July
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

AI safety nonprofit Model Evaluation and Threat Research (METR) says Anthropic may have crossed its own early-warning threshold for AI-driven research acceleration as early as July. METR released its review alongside a finding that model capabilities on selected tasks have improved about 1.9 times faster since October 2025. Anthropic’s policy treats a doubling of progress plausibly driven by automated research as a warning trigger, not proof that a specific danger has arrived. METR’s review of Anthropic’s August risk report concluded that the company’s public account understated both the estimated acceleration and the uncertainty around it. Figures in an internal version implied a rate of 1.97, METR said. Anthropic had the right to redact the review and removed most of the evidence METR considered informative, saying disclosure could help competing developers. METR also said Anthropic halted a planned audit of how it allocates computing resources between capability and safety research, choosing to focus first on risk assessment.

items.title: [thehackernews.com] OpenAI says Linux exploits cost $1,279 each, urges patching
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

OpenAI says a mid-October campaign using its GPT-6 Cyber model generated 948 working Linux kernel privilege-escalation exploits at an average API cost of $1,279 each; 588 of the targeted flaws were previously unknown. The exploits could let someone with ordinary local access gain root privileges, and OpenAI says it sent Linux maintainers 304 critical findings with proposed patches. The U.K. National Cyber Security Centre warned that AI tools are accelerating vulnerability discovery and that organizations must adapt their patching and testing processes. OpenAI introduced GPT-6 Cyber on Nov. 5 for a limited group of approved customers in its Daybreak Red program, which supports authorized advanced security testing. The model also helped identify 81 previously unknown high-severity Firefox flaws; Mozilla has begun releasing fixes. OpenAI says the model stayed within its assigned scope in 99.93% of tests without an additional deployment safety prompt, but The Register reported that OpenAI declined to detail the cases in which it crossed that boundary. Dragos tested the model in a mock power plant, where it identified two previously unknown flaws in engineering software that handles protective-relay data, according to Cybersecurity News. OpenAI has added a dedicated access group for approved critical-infrastructure defenders and says it is expanding access to GPT-6 Cyber across approved Daybreak Red customers in the coming weeks.

items.title: [indianexpress.com] OpenAI rolls out GPT-6 Cyber after Linux and Firefox findings
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

OpenAI has begun offering GPT-6 Cyber, a model designed to find and test software vulnerabilities, to a limited group of approved customers in its Daybreak Red security program. The company says researchers used it to identify 81 previously unknown, high-severity flaws in Mozilla Firefox and develop working exploits for 948 Linux kernel vulnerabilities, 588 of them previously unknown. Mozilla has released fixes for many of the Firefox issues; OpenAI says it sent Linux maintainers 304 critical findings with proposed patches. OpenAI rates the model “Critical” for cybersecurity under its own Preparedness Framework, up from “High” for its predecessor, GPT-5.6 Cyber. On the company’s ExploitGym benchmark, GPT-6 Cyber scored 48.5%, compared with 32.1% for GPT-5.6 Cyber. OpenAI says the model stayed within authorized testing scope in 99.93% of tests without a deployment safety prompt and 100% of tests with one. The model’s exploit-development abilities can support security testing or be used in attacks. OpenAI says it added safeguards including account and network controls, monitoring and reviews of high-risk activity. It plans to expand access to approved Daybreak Red customers in the coming weeks.
